hints: Look closely at what mRNA is made from, and ask yourself which of the four substances are also used to make lots of other things like DNA, ATP and proteins.
Remember that a good radioactive label must be specific. Which base is found only in RNA, and which sugar is found only in RNA and not in DNA?
walkthrough:
**What are we trying to label?**

Think of mRNA as a chain of RNA nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a ribose sugar, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base (A, U, G or C).

So all four substances could end up in mRNA, but we need one that ends up *only* in mRNA.

**Check each substance for specificity**

Adenine (1) is in both DNA and RNA, and also in ATP. Inorganic phosphate (3) is in both DNA and RNA, plus ATP, phospholipids and many other molecules.

If we used those, many tissues would become radioactive even if they were not making mRNA. They are too general.

**Pick the RNA-only labels**

Ribose (2) is the pentose sugar found only in RNA. DNA uses deoxyribose instead.

Uracil (4) is the base found only in RNA. DNA uses thymine instead of uracil. So 2 and 4 will specifically label newly made RNA, including mRNA.

options.A: Includes adenine and inorganic phosphate, which are also incorporated into DNA, ATP and other molecules, so they are not specific for mRNA synthesis.
options.B: Includes adenine and inorganic phosphate as well as ribose, but adenine and phosphate would label DNA synthesis and respiration as well as mRNA synthesis.
options.C: Correct, because both ribose and uracil are found in RNA but not in DNA, so they specifically mark tissues actively making mRNA.
options.D: Uracil alone is specific, but ribose is also specific to RNA, so limiting to 4 only misses another suitable label.
